Crick said hoops burst two or three times a year without danger; the 'warning' is a slipped hoop, not an explicit prediction of disaster.
The inquest found death 'casually, accidentally and by misfortune'; stories of people drinking themselves to death are later embellishment.

topic: SS Vestris (1928): a listing liner waits until morning to send its SOS, gives the wrong position, and capsizes before rescue ships arrive

sources.institution: US District Court, S.D.N.Y., The Vestris, 60 F.2d 273 (1932), via Justia (archived copy)
National Underwater and Marine Agency (NUMA)

cautions: The court gives 110 lives lost from 325 aboard; other counts run from about 110 to 127. Say 'more than 100'.
The cause of the initial leak was disputed (coal port vs. broken scupper or pipe); do not state one as fact.
Captain Carey's reasons for delaying the SOS are unknown; motives such as avoiding salvage costs are speculation.

topic: SS Hilda (1905): blinded by snow outside Saint-Malo, a Channel steamer strikes the rocks at night and only six people survive by clinging to the rigging until dawn

sources.institution: Board of Trade formal investigation report, February 1906 (transcribed by Histomar)
Bateaux de Saint-Malo (Saint-Malo maritime history site)

cautions: Death toll is usually given as 125; early official estimates said 128. Use 'about 125'.
Six survived: five Breton onion sellers ('Johnnies') and one seaman. Some died in the rigging before rescue.
Exact time of striking is given as around 11pm to midnight depending on source.

topic: Calne (978): England's leading councillors crash through the upper floor of the hall at Calne mid-meeting, while Archbishop Dunstan alone stays standing on a beam

sources.institution: Project Gutenberg (The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Ingram translation)
focus: stood alone upon a beam

sources.institution: British History Online (Victoria County History of Wiltshire, vol. 17)

cautions: No death toll is recorded; the Chronicle says only some were badly hurt and some did not survive.
Later hagiography casts Dunstan's survival as a miracle against his opponents; present that as a later interpretation.
Some scholars date the council to 977.

topic: Paisley Cinema (1929): at a packed Hogmanay children's matinee in the Glen Cinema, smoke from a film canister and a cry of fire send hundreds rushing to a locked exit

sources.institution: UK Parliament, Hansard (Home Secretary's written answer on the Paisley cinema disaster, 23 January 1930)
BBC News Scotland
focus: rushed for the padlocked exits

cautions: There was no actual fire in the auditorium; a nitrate film canister smouldered and smoke caused the panic.
71 children died (69 at the scene, two later). Audience size is unknown, estimated 600-1,000.
Who padlocked the exit gates was never settled at the inquiry; do not blame a named person.

topic: Vienna Ring fire (1881): minutes before Offenbach's opera, gas lamps ignite the stage, the lights go out, and the audience is trapped in the dark behind inward-opening doors

sources.institution: The Spectator, 17 December 1881 (Spectator Archive)
focus: half the doors open inwards

sources.institution: HISTORY (A&E Networks)

cautions: The death toll is heavily disputed: the official count is about 384-386, contemporary press guessed up to 900, and HISTORY gives 620-850. Say 'hundreds' or 'at least 384'.
English sources spell it 'Ring Theatre' or 'Ring Theater'; the German name is Ringtheater.
Details of exactly how the gas ignited differ between accounts; keep it to gas lighting igniting the stage scenery.

topic: Brunswick Theatre (1828): after repeated warnings about weights hung from its new iron roof, the roof fell in during a rehearsal three days after opening

sources.institution: All the Year Round (1868), conducted by Charles Dickens, retelling the inquest evidence (reproduced by An Engineer's Aspect)
focus: Pulsford, employed to survey and measure the work
Does not this alarm you?

sources.institution: Londonist

cautions: The primary is an 1868 retelling based on inquest testimony, not a same-day report; quote warnings as reported at the inquest.
Death toll is reported as 10 to 15 (13 is often given); do not state one exact number.
The inquest verdict blamed heavy weights hung from the roof; the proprietors were fined only nominal sums.

topic: William Huskisson (1830): stepping down at Parkside to greet Wellington on the railway's opening day, he was run down by Rocket and died that evening

sources.institution: Science Museum Group: letter by William Scoresby, 21 September 1830
The Gazette (official public record)

cautions: Do not call him the first person ever killed by a train; say he was killed at the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway.
He was carried to Eccles and died around 9 p.m. the same day; accounts differ on whether he clung to the carriage door or fell in its path.
Rocket was driven by Joseph Locke per the Gazette.

topic: Yarmouth suspension bridge (1845): crowds rushed to one side to watch a clown in a tub drawn by geese, rods gave way, and 79 people, mostly children, died

sources.institution: Norwich Mercury, 10 May 1845, reprinted in F. D. Palmer, Yarmouth Notes 1830-1872 (Project Gutenberg)
focus: drawn by four geese
rods were observed to give way
defect in the joint or welding of the bar that first gave way

sources.institution: BBC News

cautions: 79 died including 59 children (BBC); the newspaper's same-night count was 75 bodies recovered.
The tub was actually towed by a hidden line from a boat; the geese were part of the act.
The jury blamed a defective weld and inferior iron and workmanship.
